<reflection>
After three experiments, the fitting results show that M20 is consistently a poor fit. Among the remaining mechanisms, a group of 13 (M12, M9, M11, M18, M19, M7, M2, M1, M10, M15, M13, M8, M6) have NLL values within about 2 units of the best (M12), indicating they are all still plausible. The third experiment (high catalyst with product) made product deactivation mechanisms (M12) become the best, but substrate deactivation and other deactivation types are also close. The previous experiments varied catalyst concentration and added product, but substrate concentration has been held constant at 2.0 M. To further discriminate, we need to probe substrate concentration dependence, which can reveal saturation, substrate inhibition, and substrate-dependent deactivation.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
We propose an experiment with high substrate concentration (5.0 M), moderate catalyst (0.01 M), and no initial product. This condition tests for substrate inhibition (M7), substrate-dependent deactivation (M11), and saturation effects in simple mechanisms. At high substrate, mechanisms with second substrate binding (M7) may show a decrease in rate due to formation of a less active complex, while simple Michaelis-Menten mechanisms will approach a maximum rate. Substrate deactivation (M11) would lead to faster catalyst loss. This design is orthogonal to previous experiments because it varies substrate significantly while keeping catalyst and product at previously used values. It avoids extreme conditions that might collapse differences (e.g., very low substrate might make all mechanisms appear first-order). The high substrate condition should provide strong discriminatory power across many mechanisms simultaneously, particularly between those with and without substrate inhibition or deactivation.
</hypothesis>
